content.thinking:
I'm deciding to keep the runner fixed in place and instead move the world around it, using a pooled set of hurdle and scenery nodes that get repositioned each frame rather than relying on camera tricks.

For scenery markings, I'm planning around 30 pooled dash/post nodes that get repositioned per frame, and for hurdles, 6 pooled nodes whose position and scale I'll adjust per spawn—though I need to confirm whether the node API actually supports setScale.

I'm thinking I can avoid the setScale complexity by just creating a unit box scaled to width/height/depth with its position set at half the height, trusting the typed API for position and scale.

Now I'm working out the hurdle physics: capping hurdle height around 1.1m so jump arcs with speed-dependent gravity clear it with enough airtime window, then calculating spacing so hurdles are spaced beyond the landing distance plus reaction time at higher speeds.

For collisions, I'm positioning hurdles ahead of the runner along the z-axis based on remaining distance, with the camera fixed behind looking forward and fog concealing far-off hurdles.

I'm pooling around 8-10 hurdle nodes, reusing slots by hiding unused ones off-screen rather than toggling visibility, and generating new hurdles whenever the next spawn distance falls within 90m of the runner, removing ones that fall more than 5m behind.

For reproducibility I'm adding a seeded RNG supporting a `?seed=` URL parameter (default 12345) so restarts can replay the same hurdle sequence, placing the first hurdle at 30m and ending the run at 500m. I'm also planning moving scenery—center lane dashes spaced every 6m, scrolling based on distance traveled to simulate motion.

Rather than fight with uncertain instancing APIs, I realize a simpler trick: since the dashes, side posts, and trees are all periodic, I can just move a repeating group by `distance mod spacing` instead of regenerating positions each frame.

I'll set up one group for dashes at spacing 6, another for posts at spacing 10, and a third for trees using a wider pattern period of 20 so I can scatter varied tree positions within it — each group just gets repositioned by its own modulo offset. Node count stays manageable, around 100 total, so individual primitives should be fine without needing instancing.

For the ground, I'm using a wide dark plane with a slightly lighter track strip raised a hair to avoid z-fighting, plus thin edge lines, and relying on fog at a 150m falloff to hide the far end so I can skip building an actual finish line.

I'm structuring the runner as a group with hip pivots driving simplified capsule legs, a torso box, head sphere, and arm groups, all nested under a jump-height wrapper so the whole figure can bob while legs swing based on distance traveled, with orange torso and blue limb coloring.

For collisions, I'm comparing the runner's z-position against each hurdle's position within a tolerance window, treating jump height as clearance to decide if the runner clears or hits, and using a swept interval check against previous and current distance to avoid tunneling through hurdles at high speed.

For jump input, I'm defining state transitions: pressing jump starts the run from ready, triggers a jump when running and grounded, and restarts the run after a loss or win, though I'm unsure whether restarting should immediately jump or just reset to ready state.

I'll settle it: pressing R resets to 'ready', while jumping after game over restarts and immediately goes to 'playing' plus performs the jump, since forcing a second press would hurt usability. Now I'm defining the input handling for keydown events on Space, ArrowUp, and KeyW with preventDefault.

For the HUD, I'm placing a stats bar below the canvas and an absolutely-positioned overlay with pointer-events disabled over the canvas for the game-over state, keeping the canvas size untouched and body margin at zero.

I also need to handle the global task-state window variables, updating them each frame and marking the ready flag true after the first frame draws, with a fallback to set it right after the app initializes in case the frame loop doesn't tick immediately.

For the game loop, I'll clamp delta time to avoid spikes, and report speed as zero while in the ready/ended states but increasing while actually playing. For visuals, I'm setting a light blue sky with fog, hemisphere and directional lighting, though I'll likely skip shadows to keep things performant.

Now I'm positioning the camera above and behind the runner looking slightly downward, and designing hurdles as red-orange boxes with varying heights, sized so they fit within a track about 5 units wide.

I'm deciding to build hurdles with unit-size primitives and scale them explicitly to avoid ambiguity, starting them off-screen below the ground until spawned, and planning to track distance as a floored integer for the score display.

For win conditions I'll cap distance at 500 for the win state, and track a running best score updated both live and at the end of a run. Now I'm sketching the runner's rig using a group with torso, head, and small face details, positioning the character to face toward negative z for the run direction.

Still writing character rig and animation logic...

Now I'm building the scenery generator, laying out dashes, edge rails, and periodic posts along the track with their positions and sizes.

For trees, I'm defining repeating clusters with trunk-and-canopy pairs placed at staggered x/z offsets across periods, making sure new ones pop in far enough back to be masked by fog density rather than appearing abruptly in view.

I'm tuning fog density against exponential falloff so hurdles and trees spawn ahead of the camera but stay mostly obscured until they're closer—settling on a density around 0.025 with spawn distances tuned so pop-in happens at low visibility. Then I'm setting up the ground plane with grass and grey track colors sized to contrast against the orange runner, and starting to write the TypeScript code with strict typings for node requires.

input.summary:
I wrote the endless runner in src/main.ts. It typechecks, but I had no shell, so I never ran `vite build` or loaded it in a browser. Treat the visuals and controls as untested.

- **Gameplay:** The runner stays at the origin while the track scrolls toward the camera. Space, ArrowUp, W or a pointer click makes it jump, and it can't jump again while airborne. Jumps follow a gravity arc. Speed starts at 10 m/s and rises 0.02 m/s per metre, reaching 20 m/s at 500 m.
- **Hurdles:** They come from a pool of 10 with random heights (0.45–1.1) and random gaps. The generator is seeded: 12345 by default, or `?seed=N` in the URL. A hit sets status `lost`, and reaching 500 m sets `won`.
- **Start and restart:** The game starts in `ready` and begins on the first jump input. R restarts into `ready`. A jump input after the run ends restarts straight into `playing` with a jump. The task text was ambiguous here, so I chose that.
- **Speed value:** `speed` in the exposed state is 0 whenever the status isn't `playing`.
- **Scenery:** Lane dashes, side posts and trees scroll past, and there is fog. The runner is an orange figure built from shapes, with swinging legs and arms.
- **HUD and state:** A DOM bar below the canvas shows distance, session best and status. An overlay on the canvas shows the start prompt and the game-over or win message with a restart hint. `window.__TASK_STATE__` updates every frame, and `window.__TASK_READY__` is set after `app.ready()`.
